title: How to Stop the Third-Week Misbehavior Slide
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin identifies the third week of the school year as the point where misbehavior begins to creep upward, driven by two converging forces: the students' honeymoon ends and their initial enthusiasm fades, while teachers, assuming the class they have seen so far is the class they will have all year, relax their standards and cut corners. He traces the familiar aftermath, in which a teacher realises a month later that control is slipping, blames the students or the generation, and resigns to stress and martyrdom. Linsin insists the whole scenario is avoidable and offers three remedies: awareness that the honeymoon period is real, shrewdness in never easing up on any standard, and a commitment to continual progress because there is no stasis in classroom management. He closes by arguing that students will rise to high expectations and that the teacher's own expectations of excellence are the decisive factor.
points: Linsin locates the misbehavior slide in two simultaneous shifts: students settling back into old habits as novelty fades and teachers relaxing standards because early weeks went well.
He argues that any easing of standards is costly and hard to reverse, so the line drawn on the first day must be held with the same precision every day until the last.
His claim that there is no stasis frames classroom management as either improving or declining, requiring the teacher to push for greater progress daily.
The piece rejects blaming students, their generation or social media, placing responsibility on the teacher's own consistency and expectations of excellence.
quotes: The first is that the honeymoon ends. Students become more comfortable. Initial enthusiasm wanes.
So they relax their standards. They cut corners. They think they don’t have to be such a stickler anymore.
Eventually, a month or so later perhaps, the teacher begins to grasp that they’re losing control. They realize to their chagrin that this year is looking more and more like last year.
The honeymoon period is real. It happens every year in every classroom unless you stick to the same precise standards, rule definitions, expectations, routines, policies, and consequences.
If you let up in any area—give in, ease up, slack off—you’ll pay for it in spades. If you give students an inch, they’ll take a mile. Even if you recognize it a month later, it’s tough to reverse.
There is no stasis. You’re either getting better or you’re getting worse. You must push for more, higher, and greater progress each day.
You must stop the slide before it begins. You must draw your line in the sand on the first day of school and then hold it as if you’re Leonidas at Thermopylae.
